data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A decentralized network of small, independently operated services is often *less* resilient to correlated failure than one large service with strictly more total internal redundancy, because decentralization fragments oversight and makes systemic coupling to a shared root cause (e.g. a hypervisor 0-day, an NTP daemon bug, a shared PKI trust anchor) invisible until cascading failures manifest.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the small services are shown to use heterogeneous implementations across the full dependency stack (kernels, runtimes, cloud providers, CAs), the shared-root-cause risk drops and resilience may exceed the monolith.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If a global rollback / kill-switch can be exercised faster by the decentralized network than by the large service, the coordination advantage flips.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the large service's internal redundancy is uniform rather than diverse (same build, same firmware), it is just as correlated as the decentralized set and the claim collapses to symmetry.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Independence of operation does not imply independence of failure. Small operators converge on the same narrow set of cheap, standardized dependencies (kernel, libc, cloud hypervisor, DNS provider, CA, NTP). When a fault is latent in a shared substrate, each node fails independently *in time* but for the *same cause*; the observed non-simultaneity is then mistaken for true independence. The large service, by contrast, can afford heterogeneity budgets, in-house root-cause teams, and coordinated rollback that the small operators cannot.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
